title: Bipartite Exact Matching: deterministic polynomial time
formal: Given a bipartite graph $G=(L\cup R,E)$ with $|L|=|R|=n$, a red/blue coloring of its edges, and $k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$, decide whether $G$ has a perfect matching containing exactly $k$ red edges. The historical question asks for a deterministic algorithm polynomial in the ordinary bit encoding of $(G,k)$. An April 2026 preprint claims such an algorithm. This entry records that claimed resolution and its verification limits; it is no longer labeled as a confirmed open problem.
why: I retain and expand this entry because exact cardinality constraints can remain difficult even when unconstrained optimization is easy. It is also a useful status correction: a research catalogue should preserve the problem and the claimed advance, while distinguishing an attributed preprint theorem from a proof that has been independently checked.
definitions: A perfect matching consists of pairwise vertex-disjoint edges covering every vertex. Exactly k is an equality constraint, not an upper bound or an approximation target. This card concerns sequential deterministic polynomial time. Ordinary bipartite perfect matching in NC and Exact Matching on general graphs are separate questions.

progress.text: El Maalouly’s survey develops algorithms and reductions around Exact Matching while describing deterministic polynomial time as unresolved.
Du’s first preprint version claims a deterministic $O(n^6)$ algorithm for all bipartite graphs and describes its proof as formally verified.

Version 3 states $O(n^6)$ arithmetic complexity and qualifies the Lean result: the main theorem is reduced to eight explicit hypotheses. The claimed mathematical resolution and the formalization scope must be assessed separately.

context_blocks.text: An ordinary perfect matching assigns every left vertex to a different right vertex. Here an additional equality constraint counts how many selected edges are red. Minimizing or maximizing the red-edge count does not decide whether a particular intermediate count is attainable.

Consider two left vertices and two right vertices, with every possible edge present. Color the two diagonal edges red and the two off-diagonal edges blue. The only perfect matchings have either two red edges or none. There is no perfect matching with exactly one red edge, although one lies between the minimum and maximum attainable counts. Even this small example defeats an interval-based feasibility test.

The randomized algebraic approach encodes matchings in a polynomial and tests whether a relevant coefficient vanishes. Finding a deterministic replacement has made the problem a particularly concrete meeting point of graph algorithms and polynomial identity testing. Approximation results relax the equality constraint and therefore answer a different question.

Du’s April 2026 preprint claims a deterministic solution for every bipartite graph. Version 3 describes its Lean formalization as reducing the main theorem to eight explicit hypotheses, rather than independently checking all ingredients. The paper states that these hypotheses correspond to mathematical results proved there or in prior work. That qualification matters when assessing the original version’s stronger formal-verification wording.

review_note: Individually written from the cited primary sources. The importance assessment is editorial. New preprint proofs have not been independently verified.
answer_criterion: Establish a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm for every bipartite instance, or prove that none exists. The April 2026 claimed algorithm would establish the positive answer if its proof is valid; this catalogue has not independently verified it.

importance.reason: Exact Matching is a central derandomization test even on bipartite graphs. Its importance remains high while the recent claimed solution is assessed.

category_assignment.reason: The bipartite restriction of Exact Matching belongs with the general static graph problem; the recorded claimed resolution and uncertain status are preserved.

sentences: Bipartite Exact Matching asks for a perfect matching containing exactly a specified number of red edges.
Even a small complete bipartite graph can have attainable red counts separated by gaps.
This makes the equality constraint stronger than minimizing or maximizing the count.
The saved card records an April 2026 preprint claiming deterministic polynomial time, together with limits on its verification.
The project is therefore to explain and assess that claimed resolution of the historical question, while keeping the bipartite restriction explicit.
